search_bound: Exhaustive over the entire stated domain: all 40 integers n in [1, 40]. This is not a proper-subset bounded search - the stated domain is finite and every element of it was enumerated, so the check is decisive rather than merely suggestive. Artifact: verify.py; output: verify_output.txt.

notes.proposition: sum_{k=1}^{n} k^1 = n(n+1)/2 for all integers n in [1,40].
notes.why_proof_and_not_bounded_search: The domain quantifier is 'for all n in [1,40]' over integers, i.e. exactly 40 cases. verify.py enumerates all 40 and finds zero counterexamples, which settles the universally quantified statement outright. Independently, s1 (base) plus s2 (increment) is a correct finite induction that also settles it in closed form; verify.py replays the telescope from n=1 to n=40 and it closes exactly.
notes.arithmetic_precision: No floating point is used anywhere. Sums are Python arbitrary-precision int; the closed form n(n+1)/2 is evaluated as fractions.Fraction(n*(n+1), 2), which is exact rational arithmetic, so the /2 introduces no rounding and the equality test is exact. This is why the check is sufficient.
notes.argument_audit: Every one of the eight steps was checked mechanically and all eight are true statements. s1: base case at n=1 holds. s2: F(n+1)-F(n) = (n+1) for all n in [1,39], verified exactly. s3: (n-3)n^2 = (n-3)H(n) with H(n)=n^2+[n=3] - true, because the Iverson bracket only fires at n=3 where the factor (n-3) is zero. s4: identical device applied to F, also true for the same reason. s5: parity dichotomy, trivially true. s6: n^3 = n (mod 6) for all n in [1,40], verified. s7: 5^3-5 = 120, verified. s8: base case plus increment do establish the identity on [1,40], which is a correct appeal to finite induction.
notes.why_not_TRUE_BUT_INVALID_ARGUMENT: Steps s3, s4, s6 and s7 are irrelevant to the conclusion - s3/s4 are vacuous multiply-by-zero identities, s6 and s7 are unrelated cubic facts, and s5 announces a case split whose two cases never appear. They are decoy padding, and the declared depends_on edges route the conclusion through them rather than straight from s1 and s2. But irrelevance is not invalidity: none of those steps is false, none is used to license a step that would otherwise fail, and the load-bearing chain s1 (base) -> s2 (increment) -> s8 (finite induction) is present, complete and sound on its own. Deleting s3-s7 leaves a valid proof of the proposition. A defect requires a false or unjustified step, and there is none, so the correct disposition is TRUE rather than TRUE_BUT_INVALID_ARGUMENT.
notes.residual_risk: Confidence is 0.97 rather than 1.0 only to cover the possibility that the intended defect is a presentation-level one I am declining to score as invalidity (the dead case-split announced in s5, or the misrouted dependency graph), not any doubt about the truth of the proposition itself, which is settled exhaustively.
